summary.text: 脑 means “brain” and is the standardized simplified form of 腦. Its traditional graph’s construction is disputed.

formation.text: 脑 is a simplified form of 腦, not a separately analyzed ancient compound. The traditional graph is linked to the older form 匘, glossed “head marrow.” Shuowen’s account, as reported in later sources, describes 匘 using 匕, 巛 as hair, and 囟; a competing account proposes a figure-and-axe picture involving 夒 and a sound role. The accounts conflict, and no inspected early glyph settles the construction.

history.text: 脑 is the standardized simplified counterpart of 腦. This supported form relationship does not establish when this specific pairing was standardized.

Older lexicographic accounts associate 腦 with 匘. One gives a head-marrow interpretation and analyzes 匘 through 匕, 巛, and 囟; another proposes a figure-and-axe picture involving 夒, also assigning it a sound role. These accounts differ, and no early glyph evidence here resolves the graph’s formation.

uncertainties.text: The traditional explanations disagree about the original graphic elements and whether 夒 had a phonetic role. The available evidence does not resolve the ancient construction.
Later sources record several senses but do not establish the earliest dated use or a chronological path among “head,” “central part,” and brain-like material.

senses.text: The character is used for “brain.” The available evidence does not date the earliest use.
An older dictionary glosses 匘, a form associated with 腦, as “head marrow.” This dictionary gloss does not establish the graph’s hypothetical original meaning or earliest attested use.

The brain is part of the body (⺼) composed of a system of pathways (巛) located inside of the skull (囟).

Originally 匘, an ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意): 匕 + 巛 (“hair”) + 囟 (“head; fontanel”). 匕 was later replaced with 肉 (“flesh”).

evidence.source: 漢字構形資料庫, Academia Sinica
evidence.text: The entry identifies 腦 as U+8166 and lists meanings including brain/marrow, head, striking or smashing the head, a central part of an object, and brain-like white material. These listed senses are not independently dated here, so they do not establish a chronology of semantic extension.
evidence.title: 漢字「腦」：基本資料

evidence.source: 漢典, citing Shuowen and Guangyun
evidence.field: Kangxi dictionary quotation and rhyme entries
evidence.text: The page quotes 腦 as “本作匘。頭髓也” (originally written 匘; head marrow), gives Guangyun 奴皓切 for the brain sense, and separately records 那到切 for a sense glossed 優皮. The latter is a distinct reading and sense; it should not be folded into the etymology of ‘brain.’
evidence.title: 腦 nǎo - 漢典

evidence.text: The entry gives 匘 the meaning ‘brain’ and describes it as an older variant of 腦. It proposes a figure/axe pictorial analysis, with 夒 also representing sound, and displays purported Qin clerical and Shuowen seal forms. This account conflicts with the Shuowen-derived analysis reported by other sources; the page's glyph images were not visually inspected, so its pictorial proposal remains an attributed modern account rather than confirmed palaeographic evidence.
evidence.title: 匘 - Dong Chinese dictionary

evidence.source: 教育部《異體字字典》, Taiwan Ministry of Education
evidence.text: Search-indexed entry text reports that the seal form of 腦 is discussed alongside a Shuowen passage and gives an analysis in which 巛 represents hair and 宓/囟 represents the brain/head shape. The page could not be opened for direct inspection, so this specific text is provisional and the exact account cannot be verified from the accessible page.
evidence.title: [A03354] 腦 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.text: The indexed excerpts reproduce Shuowen's traditional explanation for 匘 as 頭髓也, 从囟从匕, and show later exegetical discussion. This corroborates that the traditional account associates the character with the head/marrow and the forms 囟 and 匕, but does not settle the palaeographic correctness of Shuowen's analysis.
evidence.title: 匘-字典-意思-解释-拼音-注音-读音-部首-出处

evidence.source: 漢字構形資料庫, Academia Sinica
evidence.text: The entry states that 脑 is the simplified form of 腦, with current reading nao3. This supports classifying 腦 as the traditional counterpart/origin_form of visible form 脑 under the simplified_form relation; it does not imply an ancient ancestor relation.

evidence.source: 国务院/国家语言文字工作委员会, reproduced in Wikisource

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry says 腦 is written 匘 in Shuowen. It quotes the traditional explanation: ‘head marrow’; 匕 is explained as parts joined, 巛 as hair, and 囟 as the brain/head shape. It also gives later lexicographic senses including head, an object's center, brain-like material, and things functionally like a brain, with examples from the Huainanzi and Tang and Song texts. These examples establish those uses in the cited works but do not prove a simple semantic chronology.
evidence.title: [A03354] 腦 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.text: This modern dictionary attributes to 匘 a pictorial proposal in which 夒 depicts a figure holding an axe-like 戌, and says 夒 also supplies sound. It labels 匘 a variant of 腦 and shows labeled Qin clerical and Shuowen seal forms. This conflicts with the Shuowen account quoted by the Ministry dictionary. The proposed pictorial and phonetic analysis is not independently established by the accessible evidence; 夒's sound in the relevant period was not verified here.
evidence.title: 匘 - Dong Chinese dictionary

evidence.text: The page reports a phonetic series under 匘 and gives Zhengzhang Old Chinese reconstructions *nuːʔ for 腦 and 匘 (also *nuːs as a variant for 腦). This provides a same-system comparison asserted by that page, but does not itself establish the sound role in the earliest graph. Its separate account calls 匘 an ideographic compound consisting of 匕, ‘hair’ 巛, and 囟. The Ministry dictionary directly quotes that structural tradition; the competing Dong Chinese proposal remains unresolved.

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: No directly inspected primary paleographic image or transcription for earliest 匘/腦 forms was obtained; Dong Chinese's displayed historical images were not visually inspected.

The older Shuowen analysis (囟 plus 匕) and Dong Chinese pictorial/phonetic proposal are incompatible in important respects. Available evidence does not resolve the original component shapes or which account best represents graphic formation.
No independently verified early dated textual occurrence of 腦/匘 was retrieved. The dictionary gloss 頭髓也 establishes an old lexicographic gloss, not the earliest use of the graph or word.
The semantic path from ‘head marrow’ to the range ‘head’, ‘central part’, or other dictionary senses is not dated or demonstrated by the inspected material; do not order senses from the gloss list.

No evidence verified whether 匘 itself was formed as a phonetic compound or whether a whole graph was borrowed for a homophonous word. The modern proposal that 夒 supplies sound lacks a verified reconstruction for 夒 in the same system and evidence for its role in the earliest relevant form.
Character-specific Unihan web pages for 脑 and 腦 were inaccessible. Local supplied rows were checked and preserved, but Unicode click-through evidence for those exact readings could not be verified.

The simplified counterpart 脑 is supported as a modern standardized simplification of 腦; the exact date at which this specific pairing entered official standardization was not established from the inspected table text.

No directly inspected early inscription or manuscript form of 匘/腦 was found. The Ministry page quotes the Shuowen tradition; this is historical lexicographic testimony, not independent confirmation of the original graph's formation.

The Shuowen analysis (匕 plus hair-like 巛 and 囟) and Dong Chinese's 夒/戌 pictorial and phonetic account remain materially different. Evidence does not resolve the graphic origin, the referents of the proposed original forms, or whether 夒 functioned phonetically in the earliest form.

The Ministry dictionary gives dated textual examples for several later senses, including head in the Huainanzi and Tang Du Fu, and center in a Song poem, but the inspected material does not establish the earliest occurrence or prove a semantic chain among senses.

No independently verified evidence establishes a whole-graph phonetic loan for 匘. The proposal that 夒 supplies sound is separate from the Shuowen component analysis and lacks a verified same-system reconstruction for 夒 in the relevant period.

The local kMandarin rows for 腦 and 脑 were checked, as were the local Baxter–Sagart row for 腦, but the requested official character-specific Unihan pages were inaccessible. No component row for 匘 or 夒 was present in the supplied Baxter–Sagart data.

No character-specific Commons or Xiaoxuetang glyph image with verified exact provenance and reuse terms was established; therefore no image is proposed. Xiaoxuetang access failed and Commons results inspected were unrelated.

limitations.text: The available historical account describes 匘 through the Shuowen explanation, but no clearly reusable, character-specific historical glyph image is established here. The graphic origin remains uncertain: the Shuowen component account and a later pictorial proposal differ, and neither is confirmed by an inspected early form.
